# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning}
**Draft 0.7.** 

This book was created to accompany students in the course *Statistics and Data Science: a broad perspective*, taught at Utrecht University. As one might expect nowadays, I have made heavy use of AI tooling throughout. But I am happy to take responsibility for the final text.

As the title suggests, my goal in this book is to cover as much of the landscape as possible. This is of course completely impossible. Therefore I have chosen  **not** to explain any of the analysis techniques, such as GLM, SEM, random forests, neural networks, etc. in much technical depth. There are already plenty of excellent books and other resources out there that do this, which are referenced throughout the text. (And, for students in the MSc program, they will be encountered in your subsequent coursework.) Instead, I have tried to put all these techniques and models into a common perspective, based on a few overarching principles:

 * The bias-variance tradeoff;
 * Explanation and prediction in social and health sciences;
 * The logic of how research questions, design, modeling, and the strength of conclusions all tie in with each other.

The latter may sound somewhat mysterious to you, so here is a summary:

> A research question motivates a design for collecting or organizing data; the design makes a set of assumptions plausible; those assumptions are the model; and the results of fitting the model answer the question, to the extent that the assumptions hold.

The chapters work through this logic. First the logic itself (@sec-rq-to-interpretation). Then, concretely, how to build a statistical model out of a theory stated in words (@sec-theory-to-glm), and what happens when the design cannot answer the question at all (@sec-identification). Then a supposedly old-fashioned idea, the analysis of variance, is rehabilitated as the gateway to multilevel models and to meta-analysis (@sec-anova). A hinge chapter steps back to ask what prediction is for (@sec-explanation-prediction). The last three chapters cross into machine learning: what overfitting is and why the bias-variance tradeoff governs every model (@sec-overfitting), how to evaluate predictions honestly, from cross-validation and the bootstrap to what happens when a well-scored model meets the world (@sec-evaluation), and what becomes of all this when there is no outcome to predict and the task is to find groups (@sec-unsupervised).

Each chapter contains two kinds of exercises. Inline exercises appear throughout; do them immediately, and click to reveal the answer below each one. The "Test yourself" exercises at the end of each chapter are harder. The practical exercises use R but, everything can be done in Python too. 

The upshot of my choice for this book is that you may sometimes like to consult other texts to get more up close and personal with a particular model. This is as things should be; my hope is that by following your own interests in this regard, it becomes possible to keep sight of the big picture and gain a "broad perspective". 

Here are a few recommendations for further study should you feel the urge. Several are open access, like this book; where they are not, I say so.

**Closest to this book.** *An Introduction to Statistical Learning* by James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani ([statlearning.com](https://www.statlearning.com/), free PDF, in R and in Python editions) covers the machine learning of chapters 6 and 7 at greater length and with more worked examples, at about the same level of difficulty. Read it first if you want more practice rather than more theory.

**Regression, and the models of chapters 2 and 4.** *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models* by Gelman and Hill is the standard treatment of the multilevel models this book reaches through the analysis of variance; its modern successor, *Regression and Other Stories* by Gelman, Hill and Vehtari, has free companion material at [avehtari.github.io/ROS-Examples](https://avehtari.github.io/ROS-Examples/). Neither book is free, but both are worth their price. For categorical outcomes, Agresti's *An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis* is the accessible entry, and his *Categorical Data Analysis* the comprehensive reference behind it.

**Latent variables and measurement.** *Latent Variable Modeling Using R: A Step-by-Step Guide* by Beaujean is a practical bridge from the equations of chapter 2 to fitted models, and the [lavaan website](https://lavaan.ugent.be/) has free tutorials for the software this book uses. For the logic of building and testing such models, Saris and Stronkhorst's *Causal Modelling in Nonexperimental Research* remains the clearest source; a revised version is in preparation and will be linked here when it is finished.

**Design and causal inference, behind chapter 3.** *Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer* by Pearl, Glymour and Jewell is the short introduction to graphs and identification; *Causal Inference: The Mixtape* by Cunningham is free online at [mixtape.scunning.com](https://mixtape.scunning.com/) and works through the designs with data and code; *Mostly Harmless Econometrics* by Angrist and Pischke gives the econometric view of the same designs. *Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference* by Shadish, Cook and Campbell is the classic on validity and design, and the source of much of chapter 1's vocabulary. More challenging, and the reference for the potential-outcomes machinery: *Causal Inference: What If* by Hernán and Robins, free at [miguelhernan.org/whatifbook](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook).

**More theory, and the deep end.** *The Elements of Statistical Learning* by Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman is the mathematical version of the machine learning chapters, freely available from [the authors' page](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/); it assumes more linear algebra and statistics than this book does. *Deep Learning* by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, free to read at [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/), goes where chapter 6 only gestures.

The book is available as a website, as a PDF sized for printing, and as an EPUB; the download links are in the sidebar. A PDF with the answers to all exercises collected at the back rather than beside the questions is at [stads-book-answers-in-back.pdf](https://daob.github.io/stads-book/stads-book-answers-in-back.pdf), and the source, the data-preparation scripts and the issue tracker live at [github.com/daob/stads-book](https://github.com/daob/stads-book).
